title: Consensus
summary:
Consensus is how a group of nodes **agrees on a single ordered sequence of decisions** (usually log entries) even though nodes crash and messages are delayed. Everyone ends up applying the same entries in the same order, so every replica of a state machine reaches the same state.

The shape is always the same: **(1)** a leader proposes an entry, **(2)** replicates it to a [quorum](#/sd/f/quorum), **(3)** once a majority has it the entry is *committed* and every replica applies it in order. Quorum overlap is what stops two different decisions from both succeeding. Families: **Paxos**, [Raft](#/sd/f/raft) and ZAB (ZooKeeper).

Guarantees:

- **Agreement and validity (safety):** no two nodes decide differently, and a decided value was actually proposed. Safety holds even if timing assumptions are violated.
- **Progress (liveness):** decisions happen while a majority is alive and can talk, and timing is reasonable. Under a partition the minority side stalls.

Costs: at least one majority round trip per decision, `2f + 1` nodes for `f` failures, and no answers without a majority.

**Use it for small, critical coordination data:** who is the leader ([leader election](#/sd/f/leader-election)), configuration, shard maps, locks and [leases](#/sd/f/lease). **Don't** run bulk data or every user click through it; replicate that normally and keep consensus for the metadata that decides who owns what.

drills.q: Which of these need consensus (not just replication)? Select all that apply.
options: Ensuring that after a failover exactly one node believes it is the database primary
Agreeing on the order of cluster configuration changes
Serving product pages from a cache
drills.explain: Both of the first two are 'everyone must agree on one answer' problems where a disagreement (two primaries, two config histories) is a correctness bug. Cached pages and view counts tolerate staleness and can be merged later.

drills.q: A 5-node consensus cluster is partitioned into groups of 3 and 2. What is the correct behavior for a client writing to the 2-node side?
options: The write cannot commit: it fails or blocks until the partition heals or the client reaches the majority side
It commits locally and syncs later
It commits because the old leader is on that side
It commits if the client retries often enough
drills.explain: Consensus picks consistency over availability on the minority side. Committing locally would create two divergent histories, exactly what the protocol exists to prevent.

drills.q: Put one decision in a leader-based consensus protocol in order.
items: The leader appends the proposed entry to its own log
The leader sends the entry to the followers
A majority of nodes have stored the entry and acknowledged it
The leader marks the entry committed
Every replica applies the committed entry, in log order
drills.explain: The entry is only committed after a majority has stored it. Applying before commit risks exposing a decision that a new leader may not have.

drills.q: A 5-node cluster has its leader in region X. Round-trip times from the leader to the four followers are 2 ms, 6 ms, 40 ms and 90 ms. Ignore disk time and processing. About how long does the leader take to commit an entry, in milliseconds?
drills.explain: A majority of 5 is 3 including the leader itself, so it needs 2 follower acks: the two fastest, at 2 ms and 6 ms. The commit completes when the second arrives, at 6 ms. Slow followers don't matter, which is why a quorum is faster and more available than 'wait for everyone' (that would take 90 ms).

drills.q: Why not make the leader wait for acknowledgements from all replicas before committing?
options: One slow or dead replica would stall every decision; waiting for a majority tolerates f failures
Followers cannot send acknowledgements to the leader
It would commit entries out of order
drills.explain: Waiting for all trades availability for nothing: a majority already guarantees any future leader's quorum overlaps with the committed entry's quorum. Safety is not the issue, availability and latency are.

drills.q: What does consensus guarantee, what does it cost, and what should you not use it for?
drills.answer: Agreement on one ordered sequence of decisions, so replicas apply the same entries in the same order and never decide differently, with progress while a majority can communicate. It costs a majority round trip per decision, 2f+1 nodes, and unavailability without a majority. Use it for small critical metadata (leader, config, locks), not for bulk data or high-volume traffic.
